name: Family logistics briefs: evening (19:30), Sunday week-ahead (18:00), weekday morning (07:00)
description: Each parent gets short scheduled texts built from the family calendar and the weather. Sunday to Thursday at 19:30: tomorrow's events, who drives, what to pack and the weather, and nothing when the day is unremarkable. Sunday at 18:00: the week ahead, with early releases, activities, drivers, packing, the weather outlook and open school deadlines. Optionally, weekdays at 07:00: weather and alerts, today's calendar, items due and trash day. Mail stays in its own digests: the school digest (F051) and each parent's 07:00 mail digest (part of G015).
example: Sunday to Thursday at 19:30 each parent gets one text: tomorrow's two events and who drives each, 'pack shin guards', and rain after 3.
how:
One isolated job per parent per brief on

-main, all from one template: tools `home_weather` plus the read-only calendar MCP (`

-calendar__*`), no web tools, no `--light-context`, `--tz` set, `--announce --to imessage:`. Schedules: evening `--cron "30 19 * * 0-4"`, week-ahead `--cron "0 18 * * 0"`, morning `--cron "0 7 * * 1-5"`. The routines and gear table lives in AGENTS.md; a run replies `NO_REPLY` to stay silent. The week-ahead and morning legs also read the household store (F031) for items due, trash day and open school deadlines. Email-derived dates for the week-ahead come from a separate

-mail job using `llm-task`, never the same run. Build the evening brief first; the morning brief is the optional one.
caveats: On Sundays the 18:00 week-ahead and the 19:30 evening brief would both arrive within ninety minutes. Either let the Sunday week-ahead carry Monday's detail and run the evening brief Monday to Thursday only (`1-4`), or accept two texts.

The morning leg is the optional one: it needs the household store (F031) for items due and trash day, and the weather plugin returns no sunset, so a sunset line, if wanted, needs a small local calculation.

If the optional 07:00 morning brief and the morning mail digest (part of G015) are both switched on, a parent gets two texts at 07:00. They cannot be one job, because the mail agent and the parent's main agent are kept apart; move one of them by a quarter of an hour, or leave the morning brief off for a parent who has the mail digest.

Dates taken from mail are not part of the first build: they would come from a separate job on the mail agent (G015, wave C), and how that job hands dates to the brief without passing email text into the parent's main agent still has to be designed. Until then the school deadlines in the week-ahead are rows a parent typed or confirmed (F010).
The National Weather Service forecast reaches seven days ahead, so the Sunday 18:00 weather outlook covers the coming week and no further.

Google's Gemini app can already send a scheduled daily digest of a person's own Google calendar, to-do list and email (being rolled out gradually to personal accounts, up to ten active actions). What Happy's brief adds is the family's own layer: who drives, what to pack from the routines table, the forecast for home, silence on an unremarkable day, and arrival in the iMessage thread.

A mute or a vacation pause (G001) is dependable only for a job that reads the paused-until row in the household store before it writes. The week-ahead and morning legs hold that tool; the evening brief as specified does not, so either add the store read to its tool list or accept that its pause rests on G001's best-effort delivery hook.
unverified: The [T]/[S] driver tag is a family habit the brief depends on, not a product feature; no source can vouch that both adults will keep it up.
gog is not installed, so its flags were checked only against its website, not a binary.
The deadlines input (home-store rows or a sheet) does not exist yet; its shape is a design choice, not a sourced fact.

The catalog passes `home-store__*` in `--tools`; the installed docs document the `<server>__<tool>` prefix only for MCP servers, and home-store is planned as a native plugin, so that glob is untested.
That the NWS forecast endpoints carry no sunrise or sunset field: the opened documentation page does not list one, absence was not proven.
The weather plugin's current fields (12-hour periods, alerts without id, no sunset) were read in ~/src/happy-config/plugins/home-weather/nws.js, which is not one of the two citable source kinds.
safety: Each brief job holds only the weather tool and the read-only calendar tool (plus the household store on the week-ahead and morning legs), has no web tool, and sends its one text only to its own parent. Calendar text can be written by people outside the family (an invitation, a subscribed feed), so it is outside content (see F009); the job's only way out is that one text to its own parent.

name: Dates into reminders and the family calendar after a yes (typed request, flyer photo or PDF)
description: After reading a flyer, slip or schedule, or on a typed request, Happy lists the dates it found, each spelled out in full, and offers reminders or family-calendar entries; nothing is written until the parent says yes. Reminders come first and need no new tool; the calendar entry is a separate, higher-risk step: a write to the family calendar with no invitees after an explicit approve, or a tap-to-add calendar file if a test shows the iPhone offers to add one from Messages.
example: Jordan sends a photo of the soccer season schedule. Happy replies with the eight game dates it read, flags one with no start time, and asks whether to set a reminder the evening before each and to put the games on the family calendar. Nothing is written until she answers.
how: Part 1, proposals (F011): a prompt-level standing order on the parent's own agent, on top of photo and PDF reading (F002) and reminders (F007); a plain conversational proposal, not `ask_user`. Optionally the bundled `llm-task` plugin returns the dates as a schema-checked list (enable the plugin, add it with `tools.alsoAllow`, list both custom model ids in `llm.allowedCompletionModels`, keep `allowModelOverride` false). Part 2, calendar write (F010): an in-house write MCP wrapping `gog calendar create` with its own write token; a `before_tool_call` hook returns `requireApproval` (10-minute cap) and rejects attendees, and the wrapper leaves delete out. A small plugin that emits an .ics attachment is built only if the tap-to-add test passes on both parents' phones.
caveats: Dates read from a photo can be wrong (a missing year, two children on one sheet, a blurry corner), so every proposal spells each date out in full and nothing is written until the parent says yes.
Until the calendar write is built the offer is reminders only; that part needs only photo and PDF reading (F002) and reminders (F007).

The yes before a reminder is a prompt rule; the approval before a calendar write is enforced by the hook. On iMessage that makes a calendar write two steps: the yes to the proposal, then a typed /approve line carrying the request's id, within ten minutes.

The tap-to-add calendar file is unconfirmed: the one report found is of a calendar file that came through Gmail and opened in Files on iOS 18 with no option to add it, so it is tested on both parents' phones before anything is built for it.
For one event on a poster a recent iPhone can already offer to add it from the camera; Happy's part is a sheet with many dates, a PDF, a day-before reminder and the calendar both parents share.
Typing /approve in iMessage Basic mode to resolve the approval was not tested end to end.
The calendar write applies only if the calendar decision lands on Google, and neither the write wrapper nor the calendar-file plugin exists yet.

A list of school deadlines or a season schedule is one more dated document: rows are stored (F031) only after a yes, and the week-ahead brief (F014) reads open school deadlines from there. A lunch menu can be read and asked about like any other photo, but no brief reads stored menu rows, and Happy is never the allergy authority.

Plugin approvals are asked once per tool call, the approval text is capped at 512 characters, and a prompt also offers 'allow always' unless the hook leaves it out. A season schedule is many events, so the write tool should take the whole confirmed list in one call, the approval text should give the count and the date range instead of every row, and the hook should offer only allow-once and deny.
corrections: A 9 Oct note says gog has no delete command. That holds only for the bundled skill text; the gog command index (gogcli.sh/commands) lists gog calendar delete, and gog calendar create accepts --attendees and --send-updates, so the write wrapper must leave delete out and strip those flags itself.

Catalog JSON 'needs' relies on ask_user for the confirmation. ask-user.md:181 says not to use it to confirm a plan, and its wait is clamped to one hour at most (ask-user.md:116-117). The Markdown already switches to a plain proposal.
unverified: That Messages on iPhone offers to add an event when an .ics attachment is tapped. Apple's guide documents .ics import from Mail and by link, and its page body could not be read by the fetch tool. One iOS 18 user on Apple's forum (discussions.apple.com/thread/255997328) reports a calendar file, received through Gmail and opened in the Files app, with no option to add it to Calendar, and a 2022 developer blog post (vadosware.io/post/how-to-import-or-open-ics-files-in-icalendar/) says only Mail and Safari offer to add one; neither covers Messages. Test on both parents' phones before building step 1; if it fails, go straight to the approved write, or try the same file by email to the asker once mailout (F049) exists.
That an .ics file passes OpenClaw's outbound media checks on iMessage (reference/rich-output-protocol.md:22) was not tested.
The in-house .ics generator plugin and the write wrapper do not exist yet.

Typing /approve in iMessage Basic mode to resolve a plugin approval was not tested end to end; the docs say channels without interactive controls fall back to plain-text /approve (exec-approvals-advanced.md:299).
Date extraction accuracy on real flyers (missing years, two children, blurry photos) has not been measured.
The calendar half has not been assessed end to end, because the write wrapper and its approval hook are not built; the reminder half needs only F002 and F007.

Which iPhones the parents carry: MacRumors' guide lists Visual Intelligence for the iPhone 16 family. Apple's own iPhone guide page for the feature returned only its menu in this review, so the phone-side claim rests on MacRumors and iPhone Life.
Whether llm-task runs with a truly empty tool surface on Happy's OpenAI provider route; the doc says the Agents API runtime may keep built-in helpers.
safety: The riskier part is the calendar write: it changes the shared family calendar, so it gets its own token, an approval enforced by a hook that fails closed, no invitees and no delete. Proposals and reminders stay on the parent's own agent and reach only the asker. Flyer text is outside content, so every write waits for a yes.

name: Happy in the parents' group chat: answers when named, and one place for shared announcements
description: Happy joins a three-way iMessage group with both parents and answers when addressed by name. In version 1 the group helper answers from weather and web search only: it keeps no memory and has no calendar or list tools, and passing a message on stays with family delivery (G009). The same chat becomes the one delivery target for announcements meant for both parents, so a watcher needs one job instead of one per parent.
example: In the parents' group Jordan writes: 'Happy, will it rain on Saturday afternoon?' and both parents see the answer. Later a storm-alert text from the weather watcher (F018) arrives once, in the same group, instead of once per parent.
how: groupPolicy allowlist with groupAllowFrom and a groups[chat_id] entry; bindings[] with peer kind group routes it to a stateless family-group agent; mention gating uses the agent name; `channels.imessage.historyLimit: 0`, so that group messages the helper skipped are not handed to it the next time it is named.
caveats: The roadmap's M1 milestone and its S1 channel-isolation baseline keep iMessage groups disabled. This entry re-opens them for one registered chat, with a sender allowlist and mention gating, so it is a change to that baseline for Tony to approve. OpenClaw's security guide calls a private room whose members you trust (team, family or friends) a normal deployment (gateway/security/access-control.md:29).

In Basic mode Happy can read and reply in a group but has no group actions such as renaming it or adding people (private-api.md:29), so a parent creates the group from a phone and Tony reads its chat id with imsg chats.
Both parents see every answer given in the group, so nothing from one parent's memory or mail belongs there; the group helper holds none.

A group that answers only when named still keeps the messages it skipped and adds them as context the next time Happy is named (channels/groups.md:547); the default window is 50 messages. Left on, what the two parents write to each other in the group would reach the cloud model in the same turn as web search results. The group history limit is therefore set to 0 (config-channels/mention-gating-and-history.md:61), so the helper sees only the message that names it.
corrections: Catalog JSON description includes a 'tell everyone dinner is at 6:30' relay and gives the group agent calendar and list tools. Neither exists on the installed stack; the Markdown already moves the relay to G009 and limits version 1 to weather and search.
unverified: Receiving and replying in a three-person group in Basic mode has not been tried live on this Mac; the docs warn that some multi-person threads arrive flagged as non-group unless the chat id is registered (access-control.md:152-153).
Whether a voice memo in the group can satisfy the mention gate on iMessage is not documented (audio.md:286 defers to channel docs).
The numeric chat id is unknown until the group is created and read with imsg chats.

That a history limit of 0 on the iMessage channel stops skipped group messages reaching the helper has not been tried on this Mac; the docs describe the window for all channels and show the key in the iMessage example config (config-channels/personal-messaging.md:172).
safety: The group helper is a separate agent with no memory tools and no calendar, list or mail tools, so nothing held by one parent's own agent can surface in front of the other. Only the two parents' handles pass the group sender allowlist, only the one registered chat is admitted, and Happy answers only when it is named. By default a group that answers only when named keeps up to 50 skipped messages and hands them to the helper the next time it is named, which would put the parents' own conversation in the same turn as web search results; the group history limit is set to 0 so that the helper sees only the message that names it. Web search results are outside content, and the helper can reply only in this group.

name: Two-parent calendar conflict watch
description: When a kid's event on the family calendar in the next 14 days falls at a time when both parents' own calendars show busy, both parents get one line naming the event and the time, once, with an optional who-covers question. Which family-calendar events count has to be a written rule (for example a tag on events that need a driver); without one the watch also flags overlaps that are no problem. Happy only reports; it moves and declines nothing.
example: Trigger: Tony accepts a Thursday 16:00 meeting; Jordan already has the dentist then, and practice is on the family calendar at the same time. Both get: 'Thursday 16:00: both of you show busy during practice. Who covers?'
how: A zero-model command job (`--command-argv`) every few hours, inside the allowed hours only, runs a host script under the happy user: `gog calendar conflicts` (or `freebusy`) across the shared family calendar and the two parents' calendars, compares against a seen-id state file, and prints `NO_REPLY` when nothing is new. To keep each parent's data separate, the script uses one read-only credential that sees the family calendar in full and each parent's own calendar as free/busy only (Google's 'See only free/busy (hide details)' share), so the message names the family-calendar event and says only 'busy' for personal ones. The docs show a single `--to` target per job, so plan one job per parent or the parents' group chat once F006 exists; the follow-up question reuses the ask-and-relay step of G009.
depends_on: F009 read-only calendar on the Google path (decision 4)
gog installed
G009 family delivery, ask-and-relay step (only for the follow-up question)
each parent shares their own calendar with the reading account as free/busy only
F006 parents' group chat, only if one job should reach both parents
caveats: Only applies if the calendar decision lands on Google; the iCloud path would need a different overlap script.
An overlap is not always a problem (both parents at the same recital). Without a rule such as 'kid event with no driver tag' it will cry wolf.
Happy reports; it does not move or decline anything.
Whether phone calendars already warn about cross-person overlaps was not checked; if they do not, this is a gap the phone leaves open.

The notification policy (G001) drops a text sent outside the allowed hours or over the daily cap instead of holding it, and by then the script has recorded the overlap as seen. So the job runs only inside the allowed hours. Timing does not cover the daily cap: a line dropped because the day's cap was reached is lost the same way, since the script cannot tell that its text was cancelled, so this watch's line either sits in a class the cap lets through or that loss is accepted and written into the job's charter.
safety: No model call, so text in event titles cannot steer anything. The calendar grant is read-only. Personal calendars are read as free/busy only, so one parent's private event titles are not shown to the other; only shared family-calendar titles appear, the same exposure as the evening brief. The message goes only to the two parents.
unverified: Flags and JSON output of `gog calendar conflicts`: gog is not installed, only its command list page was read.
How Ohai's conflict check behaves in use; its feature page says it scans connected calendars, flags overlapping events and offers to reschedule, which goes further than Happy's report-only line.
Whether `gog calendar conflicts` works on calendars shared as free/busy only.

That phone calendars give no cross-person overlap warning: a web search in round 3 found no Google or Apple help page describing one, only forum posts, so it is still not settled by an official source.
Whether one job can announce to two recipients; the docs' examples show a single `--to` target.

Where each parent's work meetings live. name: Trip and outing planner (day trip, weekend, multi-day)
description: 'Plan Saturday for us, kids 8 and 10, rain likely' returns two options with opening hours, the weather and links, and admission prices where a page could be read. A longer plan (a weekend or several days) can be emailed to the asker; hotels and transport come as links, not prices. For a trip abroad with the children the plan ends with a paperwork line: whether the passports cover the dates, and a pointer to the official page on the consent letter advised when a child travels with only one parent or without either parent. An optional Friday 16:00 job sends a 'this weekend near us' text built the same way. The parents book.
example: Jordan texts: 'Plan Saturday for us, kids 8 and 10, rain likely.' Happy answers 'on it', then sends two options, one indoors and one outdoors with a rain fallback, each with opening hours, Saturday's forecast, a link, and the admission price where the venue's page showed one.
how: One research sub-agent run via `sessions_spawn` with `runTimeoutSeconds`, composing `web_fetch`, the place lookup and `home_weather`; calendar free time crosses as date ranges only; the Friday 16:00 job reuses it. The place lookup is a tool on the research agent and one of two connections to Google's place data: the `goplaces` command that OpenClaw bundles a skill for, wrapped as a host-side stdio MCP with `GOOGLE_PLACES_API_KEY` and the home coordinates held in the wrapper, or Google's hosted Maps server (Grounding Lite), which the roadmap names. For a trip abroad the parent's own agent, not research, adds the paperwork line from the renewals table (F063) and fixed official links; passport dates and names are never handed to research.
caveats: Happy books and pays for nothing: the plan ends in links and the parents book.
Prices are best effort. Plain page reads fail on many booking, hotel and transport sites, so those come as links, and an admission price appears only when a page that could be read showed it.

The pieces arrive at different times: opening hours and ratings need the place lookup (formerly F021, now part of this entry and not built), an hour-by-hour rain line needs the weather upgrade (F083), the emailed long version needs mailout (F049) and the passport line needs the renewals table (F063). Until then the plan is built from web pages and the half-day forecast and comes back as a text.
Drive time is not part of the plan unless a route lookup is added with the place lookup.
Only ages, a place, a distance and free dates as ranges are meant to reach the research agent; that is an instruction to the parent's agent, not an enforced limit.

The paperwork line is a pointer, not a ruling. USAGov's page on travel documents for children (usa.gov/travel-documents-children) covers trips abroad and says a consent letter, preferably notarised, should come from the other parent when a child travels with one parent, and from both when the child travels with a guardian or alone. Entry rules differ by country and airline, and Happy certifies nothing.

A general assistant such as Gemini already drafts an itinerary from a typed prompt, as the Google post behind this card shows. Happy's version saves retyping the family's ages, free dates and home weather, and adds the paperwork line.

The roadmap's research milestone names Google's hosted Maps server (Grounding Lite) for place data, and OpenClaw bundles a skill for the goplaces command instead. Both read Google's place data and both need billing switched on, so one is chosen before building. Google's page says the hosted server's place search returns an AI-generated summary with place ids and Maps links and does not mention opening hours, so check first that it can answer 'is it open now?'.
For a one-off 'is it open now?' the maps app on a parent's phone is quicker and has live traffic. The place lookup is here as data for the plan, not as a separate thing to ask Happy.
corrections: Drive time was dropped from the 9 Oct wording because goplaces was thought to lack it; upstream goplaces `directions` or Grounding Lite `compute_routes` can supply it.
unverified: Hotel and train price snapshots: no opened source shows these sites are readable logged-out; expect links instead of prices.
The weather plugin returns 12-hour periods today (read in ~/src/happy-config, not citable), so an hourly rain window needs the plugin change in F083.
The emailed long version depends on the mailout server (F049), not built.
Current Places and Routes prices and free allowances were not read.
goplaces is not installed, so its flags were checked against the bundled skill and the upstream README only.
Whether Grounding Lite is generally available or a preview: Google's page does not label it.
safety: The research agent holds no family data: it is given ages, a place, a distance and free dates as ranges only (a prompt rule on the parent's agent, not an enforced limit), and it has no payment or booking tool. The paperwork line for a trip abroad uses passport dates and names, so the parent's own agent writes it and none of it is handed to research. Answers go only to the asking parent. The Google key and the home coordinates sit in the host-side wrapper, not in the prompt, and every place query goes to Google.

name: Model-free watchers on public sources: storm alerts for home, moved games and changed pages, matched recalls
description: Scripts with no model check public sources on a schedule and text a parent once when something new matters: a winter storm, wind, flood or freeze alert for home (with a chore checklist and, on a school night, a line to watch for the school's own notice), a practice or game that moved or a registered site that posted something new, or a product, food or medicine recall that matches what the family owns. Each watch is its own switch that Tony sets up; Happy does not know whether school is closed.
example: Trigger: the Saturday game's start time changes in the team's feed. Text: 'Soccer Saturday moved from 9:00 to 10:30, same field.'
how: All are operator-created host command jobs (`--command-argv`) with no model call: a script fetches a public source, keeps seen ids in a state file and prints one templated line or `NO_REPLY`. Weather (F018): `nws-alerts.mjs` every 30 minutes polls the National Weather Service active-alerts feed for the home point and dedups on the alert id. Schedules and pages (F029, SRC-09): `ics-watch.mjs`, hourly in season, reads a team's subscription link and reports changed events in the next seven days; `watch-page.mjs` every 6 hours uses a site's feed when there is one, otherwise a plain https GET and a text hash. Recalls (SRC-03, SRC-04): `cpsc-recalls.mjs` daily and `fda-recalls.mjs` twice a day, matched locally against owned-item, allergen, staples and medicine keyword lists. The schedule, page and recall jobs are timed inside the allowed hours of the notification policy (G001); only the storm-alert job runs round the clock.
caveats: A parent cannot start a watch from chat: command jobs are created by the operator, so each new watch is a request to Tony.

None of these gives earlier notice than the source's own service: Apple's Weather app can notify about government alerts once that is switched on, the team app's push is faster for a same-day change, and both recall agencies offer their own sign-ups; Happy adds the match, the school-night line and one text to both parents.
Happy is down in a power cut or a network outage and FDA's own list does not carry every recall, so silence from a watch is never an all-clear and the phones' emergency alerts stay on.
With a shared state file the second parent's job finds nothing new and stays silent, so each parent's job keeps its own file or one job delivers to the parents' group chat.

Command jobs run on the Gateway host as the happy user, outside the sandbox, agent tool policy and OpenClaw's fetch guardrails, so the scripts check each address themselves (https, public host) and are reviewed like the rest of the config repo.
A team's subscription link is a bearer secret, so it sits in a file only the happy user can read and stays out of family.json5 if that file is committed.
A hash watch on a school or town page can fire on changes that do not matter, pages that need JavaScript are out of reach, and many school portals publish no feed.

The recall match is only as good as the family's lists (substring matching gives false positives and misses unlisted items), and meat and poultry recalls and cars are not covered; parents add VINs and car seats to NHTSA's own app.

The notification policy (G001) drops a text sent outside the allowed hours or over the daily cap instead of holding it, and by then the script has recorded the item as seen, so a change found at night would never be told. The schedule, page and recall scripts therefore run only inside the allowed hours. The storm alert goes in G001's urgent class, which passes quiet hours, so a storm text can arrive in the night; if that is not wanted, the storm job can be timed inside the allowed hours as well, once a test shows that an alert issued overnight is still in the active-alerts feed at the first morning run. Timing does not cover the daily cap: a watcher text dropped because the day's cap was reached is lost the same way, since the script cannot tell that its text was cancelled, so watcher texts either sit in a class the cap lets through or that loss is accepted and written into each job's charter.
corrections: The catalog's needs used `--once` and the verifier said no CLI flag exists (JSON or Control UI only); the installed CLI source defines `--trigger-once`.
unverified: That an NWS update to an existing alert arrives under a new id pointing back through `references`: the fields were seen, their semantics were not read, so the dedup rule needs a test.
The current weather plugin returns alerts without an id (read in ~/src/happy-config, not a citable source kind), which is why the script calls the API directly.
Which alert types the Weather app's severe-weather notification covers: Apple's pages say government-issued severe weather alerts without listing them.
Which of the family's school, town and camp sites publish a feed, and which registration pages can be read without JavaScript.
The five-watchers-per-person cap is a convention; nothing enforces it.
Which agent's session transcript receives the mirrored announce line of a command job; check by reading the transcript after the first run, and keep the line short and templated.
GameChanger's exact rules on who can sync practices versus games.
How quickly each service's .ics link itself reflects a change (only the downstream calendar lag is documented).
Rate limits or terms for polling the subscription links hourly.
Formal terms of use or rate limit for the recall web service (the page read gives none).
Documentation for the RecallDateStart parameter (it is not on the API information page read; it is confirmed only by the live response).
The USDA FSIS recall API (endpoint, fields, terms): the page returned 403.
Whether the FDA RSS feed has a documented polling limit.
safety: No model reads any feed, page or recall: each script prints a fixed line with outside titles stripped and capped, and only the official or registered link. Requests go only to addresses Tony registered, and nothing about the family is sent out. Team schedules say where the kids will be, so they stay on the host and go only to pinned parent handles.

name: Meals to the grocery list: recipe links, a recipe box and a Sunday dinner plan
description: Text a recipe link and get the ingredient list and the steps, scaled to the number of people, with an offer to add the ingredients to the shared grocery list and to save the recipe. On Sunday afternoon the parent who cooks gets five dinner ideas drawn from the saved recipes and fitted to the week's calendar and allergies; a reply swaps a night or adds a dinner's ingredients to the list.
example: A parent texts: '<recipe link> What do I need for this for six people?' Or the Sunday trigger: five dinner ideas arrive and the cook replies 'swap Wednesday'.
how: Recipe link (WEB-11): the parent's own agent hands the URL to the research agent with `sessions_spawn`; research fetches the page with `web_fetch`, makes one `llm-task` call with a small schema (title, yield, ingredients, steps, source link) and returns it. The parent's agent scales quantities, proposes items for the shared grocery list (F030), written only after a yes, and after a yes saves the recipe to the recipe box: a page in the family vault (F043, its memory-wiki step, written with `wiki_apply`). Recipe text does not go into the household store (F031), whose rows are meant to stay short and typed. Sunday plan (F033): an isolated scheduled job on the parent's agent reads the saved recipes and the calendar and saves the plan, as recipe titles against days, for the main session to use when the parent replies; nothing is ordered. Pages plain fetch cannot read fall back to the research browser and the summarize wrapper (F020).
caveats: The recipe box starts empty; a recipe gets in when a parent sends a link and says yes to saving it.
The fetch returns readable article text, not the page's embedded recipe data, so the model parses ingredients from prose and can drop a line; the source link is always included.
Some recipe sites sit behind bot walls or paywalls and return nothing; Happy says so instead of guessing.
The phone's reader view and recipe-keeper apps already clean up a recipe page; the added value is the hand-off to the shared grocery list and a plan fitted to the family calendar.
Happy does not know what is in the kitchen, so it offers the whole ingredient list and the parent strikes what they have.
Scaling quantities is arithmetic done by a language model: fine for a stew, worth a second look for baking.
The reading part works the day the research agent exists; the grocery hand-off waits on the Reminders bridge (F030) and the Sunday plan on the calendar connection (F009), and neither exists yet.
The schema fixes the shape of what research returns, not its content, and nothing in the platform forces that check to run.

The allergy fit is the model reading the family's allergy notes against each recipe's ingredient list. It can miss an allergen that sits inside an ingredient, so Happy is never the allergy authority and the cook still checks ingredients and labels.

A saved recipe is text lifted from a web page, and the Sunday job and both parents' agents read it back later, so it is a place where an instruction hidden in a page could persist. It is kept as a vault page in the fixed shape the schema returns (title, yield, ingredients, steps, source link) and saved only after a yes; it is never a household-store row, which F031 keeps for short typed facts.
unverified: It depends on the calendar connection (F009) and the Reminders bridge (F030), neither of which exists yet.
The 9 Oct statement that AI meal-plan features have poor retention has no source opened in this run.
Whether web_fetch output ever includes a page's JSON-LD blocks: a search of the installed code found no JSON-LD handling in the fetch extractor, but no live recipe page was fetched.
How many of the recipe sites this family uses embed schema.org Recipe data.

Whether a plugin hook can enforce a schema on a sub-agent's result before

-main reads it.
Whether llm-task's isolated completion works through the family's per-person custom provider ids; its allowed-model list has to name them.
safety: Two agents, kept apart: research reads the untrusted recipe page and is given only an address and a serving count; the parent's own agent holds the calendar, allergies and saved recipes and cannot browse. Text returned from research, and a recipe saved from it, is still outside content, so list writes and saves wait for a yes.
